Now, as for lactose intolerance, the reason it's not its own race is... Well, actually, it is associated with particular races. It turns out most mammals don't retain the ability to digest lactose into adulthood because most mammals only drink milk as juveniles. Now, that actually includes a lot of humans, and you can actually trace the general pattern of our early development and migration. If I recall correctly, regions with particularly high levels of lactose intolerance include most of Africa, Asia, and the Americas - with the exception of descendants of European immigrants, because it turns out that the branch of humanity that grew into Europe was one of the relatively few that developed the mutation that makes us produce lactase - the enzyme that digests lactose into adulthood.

By the way, the basic reason that recessive genes are recessive is that you have two copies of each of your genes and if one of them is activated in adulthood and produces functioning lactase, your body will produce lactase, even if the other copy doesn't get activated or doesn't correctly produce lactase, and you won't be lactose intolerant. To be lactose intolerant, both copies need to shut off after childhood or otherwise broken.
